title: Separation of Duties
summary: Separation of duties is a control principle that splits a sensitive process across two or more people so that no single individual can complete it alone. It is closely related to the principle of least privilege and to the two-person rule used for physical assets, but its focus is the workflow rather than the permission set: the request, the approval, the execution and the review belong to different roles. The mechanism works because collusion is harder and more visible than a single mistake or a single act of fraud. Typical pairings include the person who writes code and the person who deploys it, the person who creates a payment and the person who approves it, and the administrator who changes a firewall rule and the reviewer who checks the change log. In practice it shows up in change advisory boards, payment approval limits, and role design in identity systems. The common mistake is implementing it on paper only; shared administrator accounts, break-glass logins used for daily work, or role assignments that grant both halves quietly collapse the control.

beginner.definition: Separation of duties means one important job is split between two or more people. Nobody can finish the whole job alone. This makes mistakes and fraud much harder to hide.
beginner.whyItMatters: One person with full control can cause harm by accident or on purpose, and nobody notices. Splitting the work adds a second pair of eyes before money moves or a system changes. It also protects the person doing the work, because a colleague confirms the decision. The cost is a little extra time and one more approval step.
howItWorks: The team lists the sensitive steps, such as creating a payment or changing a firewall rule.
Each step is given to a different role with its own named account.
One person requests or prepares the change and cannot approve it alone.
A second person checks the request against the rules and approves it.
The work is carried out, and a third person or a log review confirms the result.
Managers review the role list regularly and remove anyone who holds both halves.
beginner.example: In a hospital, the doctor writes the prescription and the nurse gives the medicine. The same person rarely does both for the same patient. If they did, a single tired mistake would reach the patient with nobody to catch it. Two people also mean two records, one for the order and one for the dose. In a company, the person who sets up a new supplier should not also approve the payments to that supplier. Splitting the task costs one extra signature and makes a quiet theft much harder to arrange.
takeaways: Split request, approval and review across different named people.
Shared accounts and everyday break-glass logins quietly destroy this control.
Review role assignments often so one person does not hold both halves.

objectives: Explain the purpose of separation of duties as a control principle.
Give examples of sensitive processes that should be split between roles.
Describe how shared or emergency accounts can undermine the control.
Outline a review process that detects conflicting role assignments.
Relate separation of duties to least privilege and the two-person rule.
